title: Water on the desert road (Acts 8:26–40)
hookLine: a powerful man with a scroll he can't make sense of, and a stranger running beside his chariot
tomorrow: what fell from Saul's eyes, and whose hands did it take?

cards: A lease, a medical form, the poem from English class everyone else seems to get: some reading is hard to do alone. Acts puts a powerful man in exactly that spot.
On the desert road down from Jerusalem to Gaza rolls a chariot. In it sits a man of Ethiopia, in charge of all the treasure of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.
He has been to Jerusalem to worship, and he's reading the prophet Isaiah aloud as he rides. The Spirit tells Philip: "Go near, and join thyself to this chariot."

teach.h: HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?
teach.b: Philip runs up and asks, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The answer is disarmingly honest: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up.
Philip "began at the same scripture," tells him about Jesus, and when they pass water by the road, the man is baptized. Then Philip is gone, and "he went on his way rejoicing."
Christians still argue about that question in the chariot.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: CLEAR ENOUGH TO READ ALONE.
teach.b: One view: scripture is clear enough that an ordinary reader can understand what matters most.
The Westminster Confession, a Reformed statement of faith, says in its first chapter that not only the learned but the unlearned can reach a sufficient understanding.
Its best case: the Bible was written for ordinary people, and nobody should need permission to open it.

teach.h: THE OTHER: READ IT WITH THE CHURCH.
teach.b: The other view: scripture is read best inside the church that carried it. Catholic teaching says the task of authentically interpreting it belongs to the Church's living teaching office.
Its best case: even a royal treasurer couldn't make sense of Isaiah alone, and a guide keeps a reader from building a private Bible. Notice what's in the chariot.

teach.h: ONE SCROLL, ONE SEAT, TWO READERS.
teach.b: The man owns the scroll and is reading it himself.
He also asks for help. Acts doesn't settle the argument. It sits both on one seat, and sends the reader home glad.

how: Christians read scripture alone and together: in personal devotions, in small groups around a kitchen table, and in church, where it is read aloud and explained.

games.q: what does “water on the desert road” mean?
o: a well where Jesus met a Samaritan woman
where a traveler from Ethiopia was baptized
the spring Hagar found in the wilderness

games.q: the chariot and the argument — tap the pairs.
p: clear enough for an ordinary reader
read it best inside the church

s: the man in the chariot couldn't read
he was reading Isaiah aloud. what he asked for was help understanding it.
Philip stayed on as his teacher
the Spirit caught Philip away, and the man went on his way rejoicing without him.
Christians still differ on how much a reader needs a guide
a Reformed confession stresses that ordinary readers can understand; Catholic teaching gives interpretation to the Church's teaching office.

games.q: your cousin reads the Bible on her own and says she doesn't need any church explaining it. what's the strongest case for the other view?
o: even a royal treasurer asked for a guide, and one keeps you from a private Bible.
the Bible is too hard for ordinary people to read at all.
only clergy are really allowed to read it properly.
games.why: the best case for reading with a guide isn't that readers are dull. the man in the chariot read Isaiah himself, and still asked: how can I, except some man should guide me?

practice: Choose one short line of scripture, or any line you carry but don't fully understand. Send it to someone you trust with one question: what do you hear in this?
Then set the phone face down for the sit, and let the line rest in you while the answer is on its way.
